description: We are a group of friends and students pursuing a University Programmer Analyst degree at UNPSJB (Comodoro Rivadavia), with a shared interest in software development.
summary:
Charmy brings together two generations of NASA satellite fire data, MODIS and VIIRS, into one consistent record. It shows that record as a burn calendar and an interactive 2D and 3D map, so anyone can see when and where fires usually happen in their area and whether this month is out of the ordinary. VIIRS sees far more hotspots than MODIS, so without harmonization a long series seems to show more fire just because the sensor changed. Charmy brings 17.5 million hotspots from five satellites since 2001 to the same scale, with a confidence interval and the source sensor for every converted month.

Behind the app, a public API serves historical hotspots, harmonized monthly calendars and validation metrics from precomputed data, and every sample value is clearly marked as provisional. Charmy also adds near-real-time detections from NOAA-20 and NOAA-21. Each detection is checked against several independent signals: satellite confidence, known fixed sources, news and citizen reports. The point is that alerts reach people only when a fire is verified, through Telegram and a CAP 1.2 feed for emergency agencies. A forecast model, published only because it beats climatology on years it never saw, shows where next month may burn more than usual. Charmy, a fire vizcacha, guides the public in Spanish and English, and a game teaches kids how a hotspot is detected and fought.
details:
Repo Link: https://github.com/cosmosnehu77/Charmy

What it does

Charmy turns more than twenty years of NASA satellite fire data into one record that anyone can read. It merges MODIS (since 2000, 1 km pixels) and VIIRS (since 2012, 375 m pixels) into a single series from 2001 to today. That covers 17.5 million hotspots from five satellites for Argentina and Chile. The record appears as a burn calendar and on an interactive 2D and 3D map of 39 provinces and regions, where height is fire. Users can explore any province, locality, rectangle or drawn polygon. They can see the typical fire season, compare this month with the historical median, follow live hotspots, check a forecast for the coming months and download the data as CSV with the same header as FIRMS.

How it works

  • Harmonization: Charmy counts fire cell-days. A 0.1° cell (about 11 km) with at least one hotspot on a given day counts as one, however many pixels or satellite passes saw it. This shrinks the resolution gap between sensors. What remains is corrected with a log-scale linear fit per region and month over the years when the sensors overlap. Industrial and gas-flare sources (370 cells) and low-confidence detections are removed first. Each converted month carries a confidence interval and the sensor it came from.
  • Validation: In cross-validation, MODIS→VIIRS reaches a median r² of 0.90 across regions and NOAA-20→VIIRS reaches 0.94. Charmy also reproduces well-known events. Corrientes 2022 shows about 10 times the median. February 2023 is the highest month in the whole series for Biobío, Chile.
  • Live hotspots: NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 detections are checked against several independent signals: satellite confidence, known fixed sources, news from the province and reports from people nearby. A language model only labels headlines. The verdict comes from fixed rules over all the signals. Local weather from Meteomatics and the clearest recent Sentinel-2 image from Copernicus add context.
  • Alerts: Only verified fires trigger alerts, sent through Telegram groups for each area and a CAP 1.2 feed for emergency agencies. Tapping a button in an alert updates its status instantly.
  • Forecast: A model gives the chance of fire in each cell for the coming months. A horizon is published only if it beats climatology on years the model never saw. At one month, it improves the Brier score by 13% over climatology.

Benefits and intended impact

Without harmonization, a long fire series seems to show more fire just because the sensor changed. Charmy removes that artifact, so trends and anomalies can be trusted. Fire crews, researchers and local agencies get a consistent record, an expert mode with validation per region and a public API. Ordinary people get a simple answer: is this normal for my area, and is something burning near me now? Every alert says that Charmy does not replace emergency services and gives the number to call.

Tools and languages

  • Data: Python 3.12, Polars, DuckDB, GeoPandas and Parquet, published as versioned GitHub releases with checksums.
  • API: FastAPI, Postgres (Supabase) and an OpenAPI 3.1 contract with a mock.
  • App: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind, MapLibre GL, Terra Draw and Observable Plot.
  • Landing and game: Astro and GSAP for the landing, PixiJS for the game.
  • Forecast: LightGBM.
  • Alerts: a Telegram bot and an OASIS CAP 1.2 feed.
  • Platform: a pnpm/Turborepo and uv monorepo, GitHub Actions, Cloudflare Pages and Docker on Render.
  • Data sources: NASA FIRMS, Meteomatics and Copernicus Data Space, called only from the server.

What makes it creative

  • A guide: Charmy, a fire vizcacha, guides the public through the map, explains each province and speaks in the second person, briefly and without alarmism.
  • A game: Charmy Brigada teaches how a hotspot is detected and fought, with wind, water, planes and firebreaks on a 3D map.
  • How we built it: five people, each with their own coding agent, worked on a shared message board with clear ownership of folders and contracts. In 36 hours that added up to over 200 merged pull requests and over 750 automated tests.

What we considered

  • Scientific honesty: Charmy measures burning activity, not burned area, and says so. Sample values are always marked, and the limits of the method are documented.
  • Responsible AI: no AI in the data or the harmonization. In live verification, AI only labels headlines and never decides a verdict alone.
  • Reliability: if an external source fails, that part shows as unavailable and the rest keeps working.
  • Security: API keys never reach the browser, and the repository has been public since the first commit without a single key in its history.
  • Accessibility: Spanish and English, light and dark themes, color-blind-safe color ramps and a layout that works on a phone.
